◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Git isn't optional in data work anymore. Every dbt project lives in Git. Every code review happens through Git. Every analytics engineer is expected to navigate branches, commits, and pull requests like breathing. Without Git fluency you cannot collaborate, deploy, or roll back changes safely. This is the single most leveraged skill in your career path.

What Git actually is

Git is a distributed version control system. It tracks every change to every file in a folder over time. You can see what changed, when, by whom, and rewind to any previous state. Multiple people can work on the same files in parallel, and Git merges their changes intelligently.

GIT'S MENTAL MODEL
Git stores snapshots of your whole project, not diffs.

Every commit = a snapshot of all tracked files at that moment.
Storage is cheap because identical files share data.

Git vs GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket

This trips up everyone at first. They're different things:

Git The tool itself. Runs locally on your computer. Open source. CLI-based.
GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket Web platforms that host Git repositories online. Add UI, pull requests, CI/CD, issue tracking on top.

You use Git locally, then push your work to GitHub (or GitLab/Bitbucket) so others can pull it. The Git commands are the same regardless of which host you use.

Installing Git

# macOS — via Homebrew
brew install git

# Windows — download from git-scm.com
# Or use winget
winget install --id Git.Git -e

# Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)
sudo apt update && sudo apt install git

# Verify install
git --version
# git version 2.43.0

One-time configuration

Tell Git who you are. These show up in every commit you make:

git config --global user.name "Natasha Smith"
git config --global user.email "natasha@school.edu"

# Set your default branch name to "main" (modern convention)
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Useful: better diff coloring
git config --global color.ui auto

# Check your config
git config --list
★ KEY INSIGHT

The email you set should match your GitHub email, or commits won't be linked to your GitHub profile. Use the same email everywhere.

Your first repository

# Make a new project folder
mkdir my-first-repo
cd my-first-repo

# Initialize Git
git init
# Initialized empty Git repository in .../my-first-repo/.git/

# Make a file
echo "# My First Repo" > README.md

# Check what Git sees
git status
# Untracked files:
#   README.md

That hidden .git/ folder is where Git stores everything. Never delete it — it's your entire history.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Starting a dbt project
cd ~/projects
mkdir my-dbt-project
cd my-dbt-project
git init
# Add dbt_project.yml, models/, etc.
git add .
git commit -m "Initial dbt project structure"
# Later: push to GitHub for the team
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Git = local distributed version control tool
  • GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket = web platforms that host Git repos
  • Git stores snapshots, not diffs
  • Configure name + email once globally before your first commit
  • The .git/ folder holds your entire history — never delete it
  • Default to main as your primary branch name

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Git's three-state model is the single most important mental model in version control. Every command you'll run either moves files between these three areas or queries their state. Master this and Git stops being mysterious.

The three states

THE THREE AREAS
1. Working Directory — the actual files you edit
2. Staging Area (Index) — files marked for next commit
3. Repository (.git/) — committed snapshots, the permanent history

Files move through these stages:

  Working Directory          Staging              Repository
       (edit)                  (stage)              (commit)
        |                        |                     |
        |-- git add file.txt --->|                     |
        |                        |-- git commit ----->|
        |                        |    -m "message"    |

Checking state: git status

git status is the command you'll run more than any other. It shows what's where:

git status

# On branch main
# Changes to be committed:           ← staged, ready to commit
#   (use "git restore --staged ..." to unstage)
#         new file:   stg_users.sql
#
# Changes not staged for commit:     ← modified, not yet staged
#   (use "git add ..." to update what will be committed)
#         modified:   dbt_project.yml
#
# Untracked files:                   ← Git doesn't know about these
#   (use "git add ..." to include in what will be committed)
#         new_model.sql

Staging changes with git add

# Stage one file
git add stg_users.sql

# Stage all changes
git add .

# Stage all .sql files only
git add "*.sql"

# Stage interactively (chunks within a file)
git add -p

# Unstage (move back from staging to working dir)
git restore --staged stg_users.sql
★ STAGING IS A SUPERPOWER

The staging area lets you commit only PART of your changes. If you've edited 5 files for two different fixes, you can stage just the files for fix #1, commit, then stage and commit fix #2. Clean history.

Committing

A commit captures the current staged state as a permanent snapshot with a message:

# Commit with inline message (most common)
git commit -m "Add stg_users staging model"

# Commit with a longer message (opens your editor)
git commit

# Stage and commit all TRACKED files in one shot (skips untracked)
git commit -am "Quick fix to typo in description"

Writing good commit messages

Commit messages are read by future you and your team. Convention:

# Format:
<type>: <short summary, imperative mood, <72 chars>

<optional longer body explaining WHY>

# Examples:
feat: add stg_users incremental model
fix: correct date filter in fct_orders
refactor: split int_user_metrics into staging + intermediate
docs: add column descriptions for dim_product
test: add unique test on orders.order_id
⚠ ANTI-PATTERNS
  • "fixes" — fixes WHAT?
  • "asdf" — please.
  • "updated some stuff" — useless in 6 months
  • "wip" — fine for personal branches, never on main
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A clean commit
$ git status
On branch main
Untracked files:
        models/staging/stg_orders.sql

$ git add models/staging/stg_orders.sql
$ git status
Changes to be committed:
        new file:   models/staging/stg_orders.sql

$ git commit -m "feat: add stg_orders staging model"
[main a1b2c3d] feat: add stg_orders staging model
 1 file changed, 28 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 models/staging/stg_orders.sql
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Three areas: Working Directory → Staging → Repository
  • git status shows what's where
  • git add stages files (moves them to staging)
  • git commit snapshots staged files into permanent history
  • Staging lets you commit partial changes cleanly
  • Write commit messages in imperative mood, under 72 chars
  • Use prefixes (feat, fix, refactor, docs, test) for clarity

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Once you have commits, you'll constantly ask: "what changed in this commit?" "When did this bug appear?" "Why is this line here?" These three commands answer all of that. They're how you investigate history — essential when debugging dbt models or auditing code changes.

git log — browse history

# Show all commits, newest first
git log

# commit a1b2c3d4e5f6 (HEAD -> main)
# Author: Natasha Smith 
# Date:   Mon May 16 14:30:00 2026 -0700
#
#     feat: add stg_users staging model
#
# commit f0e9d8c7b6a5
# Author: Natasha Smith 
# Date:   Sun May 15 09:12:00 2026 -0700
#
#     Initial dbt project structure

# Compact one-line view
git log --oneline
# a1b2c3d feat: add stg_users staging model
# f0e9d8c Initial dbt project structure

# With branch graph
git log --oneline --graph --all

# Limit to last 5 commits
git log -5

# Show commits by an author
git log --author="Natasha"

# Commits touching a specific file
git log -- models/staging/stg_users.sql

# Search commit messages
git log --grep="incremental"

# Show what changed (full diff per commit)
git log -p

git diff — see what changed

git diff compares states. Default: working directory vs staging.

# Working dir vs staging (what's NOT staged)
git diff

# Staging vs last commit (what WILL be committed)
git diff --staged
# (or --cached, same thing)

# Working dir vs last commit (all uncommitted changes)
git diff HEAD

# Compare two commits
git diff a1b2c3d f0e9d8c

# Diff for a specific file
git diff models/staging/stg_users.sql

# Diff against another branch
git diff main..feature/incremental

Reading a diff:

diff --git a/dbt_project.yml b/dbt_project.yml
index 1a2b3c4..5d6e7f8 100644
--- a/dbt_project.yml          ← "a/" = old version
+++ b/dbt_project.yml          ← "b/" = new version
@@ -10,3 +10,4 @@                ← line numbers
 name: my_project
 version: '1.0.0'
-profile: 'dev'                  ← "-" = removed
+profile: 'analytics_dev'        ← "+" = added
+vars:                           ← "+" = added

git show — inspect one commit

# Show full details of a commit
git show a1b2c3d

# Show just the file list changed
git show --stat a1b2c3d

# Show a specific file from a specific commit
git show a1b2c3d:models/staging/stg_users.sql

# Show the latest commit
git show HEAD

# Show 2 commits ago
git show HEAD~2
★ HEAD AND COMMIT REFERENCES

HEAD = the current commit you're on. HEAD~1 = one commit before. HEAD~3 = three commits before. Use commit hashes (a1b2c3d) for specific commits. Even 7 characters of a hash is usually unique enough.

git blame — who wrote this line?

# Show who last modified each line of a file
git blame models/marts/fct_orders.sql

# a1b2c3d4 (Natasha 2026-05-16 14:30:00) select
# a1b2c3d4 (Natasha 2026-05-16 14:30:00)     order_id,
# f0e9d8c7 (Sarah    2026-05-10 09:12:00)     customer_id,
# f0e9d8c7 (Sarah    2026-05-10 09:12:00)     order_date,
# a1b2c3d4 (Natasha 2026-05-16 14:30:00)     amount

# Blame for specific line range
git blame -L 10,20 models/marts/fct_orders.sql
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Investigating a broken model
# Your dbt run is failing on fct_orders. When did it break?

# 1. See recent commits touching the file
git log --oneline -- models/marts/fct_orders.sql
# a1b2c3d refactor: simplify fct_orders join logic
# f0e9d8c feat: add fct_orders mart

# 2. Look at what changed in the suspect commit
git show a1b2c3d

# 3. Find who introduced the broken line
git blame models/marts/fct_orders.sql

# Now you know who wrote it, when, and why (commit msg)
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • git log = browse commit history (use --oneline, --graph, --author)
  • git diff = compare states (default: working vs staging)
  • git diff --staged = preview what will be committed
  • git show <hash> = inspect a specific commit fully
  • git blame <file> = find who last touched each line
  • HEAD = current commit; HEAD~N = N commits ago
  • 7+ char prefix of a commit hash is enough to reference it

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Mistakes happen. You'll stage the wrong file, commit a typo, or want to throw away an experiment. Git has a tool for every undo scenario — most of them safe, a few destructive. Learn which is which now, before you lose work.

The undo decision tree

WHICH UNDO DO YOU NEED?
Staged but want to unstage? → git restore --staged <file>
Modified but want to discard? → git restore <file> (⚠ destroys edits)
Committed but want to amend message/files? → git commit --amend
Want to undo a commit but keep changes? → git reset --soft HEAD~1
Want to throw away a commit entirely? → git reset --hard HEAD~1 (⚠ destructive)
Want to revert a commit safely on a shared branch? → git revert <hash>

Unstaging files

# You did git add by accident; want to unstage:
git restore --staged models/staging/stg_users.sql

# The file is now back in "modified" state
# Your edits are NOT lost — just unstaged

Discarding working-directory changes

# Discard all unstaged changes to a file (⚠ DESTRUCTIVE)
git restore models/staging/stg_users.sql

# Discard ALL unstaged changes everywhere
git restore .

# Older syntax (still works)
git checkout -- models/staging/stg_users.sql
⚠ THIS THROWS AWAY EDITS

git restore <file> destroys any unstaged edits permanently. There is no undo. Use only when you're sure you want to ditch the changes.

Amending the last commit

Forgot to add a file? Typo in the commit message? Amend before you push:

# Add forgotten file to the last commit
git add forgotten_file.sql
git commit --amend --no-edit
# (--no-edit keeps the existing message)

# Or change the message of the last commit
git commit --amend -m "feat: add stg_users with correct typing"
⚠ NEVER AMEND AFTER PUSHING

Amending rewrites the commit. If you've already pushed, you'll have to force-push, which breaks teammates' clones. Only amend local commits not yet pushed.

Three flavors of reset

# Undo the last commit, KEEP the changes staged
git reset --soft HEAD~1
# (commit gone, changes in staging — ready to recommit)

# Undo last commit, KEEP changes in working dir (unstaged)
git reset HEAD~1
# (commit gone, files modified but not staged — default behavior)

# Undo last commit AND throw away the changes (⚠ DESTRUCTIVE)
git reset --hard HEAD~1
# (commit gone, files reverted, changes lost)

# Reset by 3 commits
git reset --hard HEAD~3

The reflog — your safety net

Even after a destructive operation, Git keeps a hidden log of every move your HEAD made. You can almost always recover lost commits via reflog:

git reflog

# a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
# f0e9d8c HEAD@{1}: commit: feat: add stg_users  ← "lost" commit!
# c4d5e6f HEAD@{2}: commit: Initial dbt project

# Recover the "lost" commit
git reset --hard f0e9d8c
# or
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
★ REFLOG IS LOCAL ONLY

Reflog records HEAD movements on your machine for ~90 days. It doesn't sync to GitHub. If you delete the repo or run git gc, reflog goes too. Still, for most "oh no" moments, reflog saves you.

git revert — safe undo on shared branches

git reset rewrites history. On a shared branch (like main after a merge), use git revert instead — it creates a NEW commit that undoes a previous one:

# Revert commit a1b2c3d safely
git revert a1b2c3d

# A new commit is created with message:
# "Revert 'feat: add stg_users staging model'"
# History stays linear, no force-push needed
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Recovering from "I just committed garbage"
# You committed test data to dbt seeds, realize 5 min later

# OPTION 1: Just made the commit, haven't pushed
git reset --soft HEAD~1     # undo commit, keep changes staged
git restore --staged seeds/test_data.csv  # unstage
git restore seeds/test_data.csv  # discard the file edits (⚠)
# Now recommit clean

# OPTION 2: Already pushed to a feature branch (no one else uses)
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git push --force-with-lease   # safer than --force
# Branch history is clean

# OPTION 3: Pushed to main (shared!) — DO NOT reset
git revert HEAD              # makes a new "undo" commit
git push                     # clean, no force needed
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • git restore --staged <file> = unstage (safe)
  • git restore <file> = discard unstaged edits (⚠ destructive)
  • git commit --amend = fix the last commit (only if not pushed)
  • git reset --soft HEAD~1 = undo commit, keep staged
  • git reset --hard HEAD~1 = undo commit + throw away (⚠ destructive)
  • git reflog = your "I made a horrible mistake" safety net
  • git revert <hash> = safe undo for shared branches (creates new commit)
  • Never amend or reset commits you've already pushed to a shared branch

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Branches are how all real team Git work happens. Every feature, fix, or experiment lives on its own branch. No one commits directly to main. Branches are cheap, fast, and isolated — once you're comfortable creating and switching between them, your workflow transforms.

What a branch is

A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit. That's it. When you commit, the branch pointer moves forward. When you switch branches, your working directory updates to match that branch's latest commit.

BRANCHES = POINTERS
Each commit has parents, forming a graph.

A branch is just a name pointing to one commit in the graph.
HEAD points to the branch you're currently on.

Creating and switching branches

# Create a new branch (doesn't switch to it)
git branch feature/add-incremental-orders

# Switch to a branch
git switch feature/add-incremental-orders

# Create AND switch in one command (most common)
git switch -c feature/add-incremental-orders

# Older syntax (still works)
git checkout -b feature/add-incremental-orders

# Switch back to main
git switch main

# Switch to the previously checked-out branch
git switch -

Listing branches

# Show local branches (* marks current)
git branch
#   feature/add-incremental-orders
# * main

# Show local + remote branches
git branch -a
#   feature/add-incremental-orders
# * main
#   remotes/origin/main
#   remotes/origin/feature/old-experiment

# Show branches with last commit
git branch -v

# Show merged branches (safe to delete)
git branch --merged

# Show unmerged branches
git branch --no-merged

Deleting branches

# Delete a merged branch (safe)
git branch -d feature/old-feature

# Delete a branch even if unmerged (⚠ may lose commits)
git branch -D feature/abandoned-experiment

# Delete a remote branch
git push origin --delete feature/old-feature

Branch naming conventions

Most teams use prefixes to organize branches:

feature/<name> New work — feature/add-stg-users, feature/incremental-orders
fix/<name> Bug fixes — fix/null-handling-in-fct-orders
refactor/<name> Cleanup — refactor/split-int-metrics
docs/<name> Documentation — docs/add-column-descriptions
chore/<name> Maintenance — chore/upgrade-dbt-1.7
★ INCLUDE TICKET NUMBERS

If your team uses Jira/Linear/GitHub Issues, prefix with the ticket: feature/DATA-123-add-orders-mart. Auto-links commits to tickets.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Starting a dbt feature
# You need to add an incremental fact table

# 1. Make sure main is up to date
git switch main
git pull

# 2. Branch off
git switch -c feature/DATA-456-incremental-orders

# 3. Build the model
# ... edit models/marts/fct_orders.sql ...

# 4. Commit your work
git add models/marts/fct_orders.sql
git commit -m "feat(DATA-456): make fct_orders incremental"

# 5. Push branch to GitHub
git push -u origin feature/DATA-456-incremental-orders

# 6. Open PR on GitHub → merge → branch auto-deleted
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • A branch is a movable pointer to a commit
  • git switch -c <name> creates and switches in one step
  • git branch lists local branches; -a shows remotes too
  • git branch -d deletes merged branches safely
  • Use prefixes: feature/, fix/, refactor/, docs/, chore/
  • Include ticket numbers when applicable
  • Never commit directly to main on a team

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Merging brings work from one branch into another — typically your feature branch into main. Understanding how Git decides between fast-forward and three-way merges, and how to resolve conflicts, is the difference between confidently shipping work and panicking when red text appears.

What merging does

Merging combines the histories of two branches into one. Git has two strategies:

FAST-FORWARD vs THREE-WAY
Fast-forward: target branch hasn't moved — just slide its pointer forward.

Three-way: both branches have new commits — Git creates a new "merge commit" combining them.

Fast-forward merge

# main hasn't moved since you branched off
# Before:
# main:    A---B
#               \
# feature:       C---D

# Merge feature into main
git switch main
git merge feature

# After (fast-forward):
# main:    A---B---C---D
# feature:         C---D

# Linear history, no merge commit

Three-way merge

# main moved while you worked on feature
# Before:
# main:    A---B---E---F
#               \
# feature:       C---D

# Merge feature into main
git switch main
git merge feature

# After (three-way):
# main:    A---B---E---F---M
#               \         /
# feature:       C-------D
#
# M is the "merge commit" — has two parents

Forcing no-fast-forward

Many teams prefer always having a merge commit, even when fast-forward is possible — it preserves the fact that the work happened on a feature branch:

git merge --no-ff feature
# Creates a merge commit even if FF was possible
# Result: explicit "this is when feature/X joined main"

Merge conflicts

When both branches modified the same line of the same file, Git can't auto-merge. It marks the file as conflicted and pauses the merge:

git merge feature
# Auto-merging models/marts/fct_orders.sql
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in models/marts/fct_orders.sql
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

git status
# Unmerged paths:
#   both modified:   models/marts/fct_orders.sql

Open the conflicted file. Git inserts conflict markers:

select
    order_id,
<<<<<<< HEAD                    ← your version (current branch)
    customer_id,
    order_date,
=======                              ← divider
    customer_id::int as customer_id,
    order_date::date as order_date,
>>>>>>> feature                  ← incoming version
    amount
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

Resolving the conflict

# 1. Edit the file — pick one side, the other, or combine
# Remove the <<<, ===, >>> markers

# 2. Stage the resolved file
git add models/marts/fct_orders.sql

# 3. Continue the merge
git commit
# Git pre-fills a merge commit message; just save and close

# Or, if you want to give up:
git merge --abort
# Returns you to pre-merge state
★ USE A MERGE TOOL

Visual merge tools make conflict resolution much easier. VS Code has one built-in (click "Resolve in Merge Editor"). For CLI fans: git mergetool launches your configured tool (vimdiff, meld, kdiff3).

Common conflict patterns in dbt

  • Same model edited by two PRs — manually merge the logic
  • schema.yml column order — usually safe to keep both
  • dbt_project.yml — usually want both sets of changes
  • packages.yml version — pick the newer compatible version
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Merging a feature branch
# 1. Update main
git switch main
git pull origin main

# 2. Merge feature in
git merge --no-ff feature/incremental-orders

# 3. Conflict in fct_orders.sql
# Edit file, remove markers, keep logic from both

# 4. Stage and complete
git add models/marts/fct_orders.sql
git commit
# Editor opens with default merge message — save & exit

# 5. Verify
git log --oneline --graph -10

# 6. Push
git push origin main
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Fast-forward: target hasn't moved, just slide the pointer
  • Three-way merge: creates a merge commit when both branches diverged
  • --no-ff always creates a merge commit (preserves branch history)
  • Conflicts happen when both branches edit the same line
  • Conflict markers: <<<<<<< HEAD ... ======= ... >>>>>>> branch
  • Resolve by editing, staging with git add, then git commit
  • git merge --abort to bail out cleanly
  • Use VS Code or git mergetool for easier visual resolution

Exercise form: concluding a merge after fixing conflicts — git add the resolved files, then git commit (or git merge --continue) to create the merge commit.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Rebase rewrites history. It makes your feature branch look like you developed it in a clean, linear sequence on top of the latest main. Used right, it produces beautiful, readable history. Used wrong, it corrupts shared branches and angers teammates. Knowing when to rebase vs merge is a senior-engineer skill.

What rebase does

Rebase takes your branch's commits and replays them on top of another branch. Result: linear history, no merge commits.

REBASE = REPLAY ON NEW BASE
Before: feature commits attached to old main

After: feature commits look like they were made on top of CURRENT main 
# Before rebase:
# main:    A---B---E---F
#               \
# feature:       C---D

# git switch feature
# git rebase main

# After rebase:
# main:    A---B---E---F
#                       \
# feature:               C'---D'
#
# C and D are REPLAYED as C' and D' on top of F
# (different commits with new hashes!)

Why rebase?

  • Linear history — easier to read with git log
  • Up-to-date branch — your work on current main before merging
  • No merge noise — no "Merge branch main into feature" commits cluttering history
  • Cleaner PRs — reviewers see your commits, not merge artifacts

Basic rebase workflow

# You're on feature/incremental-orders
# Main has moved while you worked
# Update your branch:

git switch feature/incremental-orders
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# If conflicts: resolve, then
git add <resolved files>
git rebase --continue

# To bail out:
git rebase --abort
⚠ THE GOLDEN RULE OF REBASE

Never rebase commits that have been pushed and others may have based work on. Rebasing changes commit hashes, which breaks anyone who pulled the original commits. Only rebase your own private feature branch.

Interactive rebase — cleaning up before PR

Interactive rebase lets you edit, reorder, squash, or drop commits before merging:

# Edit the last 4 commits
git rebase -i HEAD~4

# Git opens an editor:
# pick a1b2c3d feat: scaffold fct_orders
# pick e4f5g6h fix typo
# pick h7i8j9k actually fix the join
# pick l0m1n2o final tweak

# Change "pick" to one of:
#   p, pick   = use commit
#   r, reword = use commit, edit the message
#   e, edit   = use commit, pause for amend
#   s, squash = combine with previous commit
#   f, fixup  = like squash, discard this msg
#   d, drop   = remove commit entirely

Squashing commits

The most common interactive rebase use: combine many "wip" commits into one clean commit:

# Before:
# pick a1b2c3d feat: scaffold fct_orders
# pick e4f5g6h fix typo
# pick h7i8j9k actually fix the join
# pick l0m1n2o final tweak

# After editing:
# pick   a1b2c3d feat: scaffold fct_orders
# fixup  e4f5g6h fix typo                  ← merged into commit above
# fixup  h7i8j9k actually fix the join     ← merged into commit above
# fixup  l0m1n2o final tweak               ← merged into commit above

# Save, exit — 4 commits become 1:
# feat: scaffold fct_orders

Force-pushing rebased branches

After rebasing a branch you already pushed, you must force-push:

# DANGEROUS — overwrites remote without checks
git push --force

# SAFE — fails if someone else pushed since you last fetched
git push --force-with-lease
★ ALWAYS USE --force-with-lease

Plain --force destroys anything on the remote. --force-with-lease checks that the remote hasn't moved since your last fetch — if someone else pushed, your force-push is rejected. Saves you from accidentally clobbering teammates' work.

Rebase vs Merge — when to use each

Use REBASE when: Updating your private feature branch with main's latest; cleaning up messy commits before PR
Use MERGE when: Integrating feature into main; combining work from shared branches; preserving merge context
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Clean PR preparation
# Your feature branch has 7 messy "wip" commits
# Main has moved while you worked

# 1. Update with latest main
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# Resolve any conflicts

# 2. Squash messy commits
git rebase -i origin/main
# Squash all into 1-3 logical commits with clean messages

# 3. Force-push (your branch only, not main!)
git push --force-with-lease

# 4. Open PR — reviewers see clean, focused commits
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Rebase = replay your commits on top of a different base
  • Creates new commit hashes (commits are rewritten)
  • Produces linear history without merge commits
  • GOLDEN RULE: never rebase shared/pushed branches others may have based work on
  • git rebase -i lets you reword, squash, fixup, drop commits
  • After rebasing a pushed branch, use git push --force-with-lease
  • Rebase your feature; merge into main

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Two scenarios you'll hit often: "I need this one commit from another branch but not the rest" (cherry-pick) and "I have uncommitted work but need to switch branches NOW to fix something" (stash). Both are simple commands that save the day.

git cherry-pick

Take one specific commit from another branch and apply it to your current branch.

# On main; want commit a1b2c3d from feature/experimental
git switch main
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d

# The commit is now on main as a NEW commit
# (different hash, same changes + message)

# Cherry-pick multiple commits
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d e4f5g6h h7i8j9k

# Cherry-pick a range (exclusive of start)
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d..h7i8j9k

# If conflicts: resolve, then
git add <files>
git cherry-pick --continue

# To abort:
git cherry-pick --abort

Common cherry-pick use cases

  • Hotfix to multiple branches — cherry-pick a fix from main into a release branch
  • Salvage commits from abandoned branches — grab just the good parts
  • Backport changes — apply a fix from main to an older supported version
  • Move a commit to a different branch — wrong branch? cherry-pick to right one, then drop original
⚠ CHERRY-PICK CAUTIONS
  • Creates duplicate commits (different hashes, same changes) — appears twice in history
  • Can cause confusing diffs if cherry-picked commit depends on un-picked context
  • Best for self-contained commits (refactors, fixes); avoid for series of related changes

git stash — save work-in-progress

You're mid-edit when something urgent comes up. You can't commit broken code, can't switch branches with dirty files. Stash to the rescue:

# Stash all uncommitted changes (tracked files)
git stash

# Or with a message
git stash push -m "WIP: refactoring fct_orders join"

# Stash including untracked files
git stash -u

# Working dir is now clean — switch branches freely
git switch hotfix
# ...fix something...
git switch -

# Restore your stashed work
git stash pop
# (pops the latest stash off the stack — applies + deletes it)

Stash stack

You can have multiple stashes simultaneously. Git stores them as a stack:

# List all stashes
git stash list
# stash@{0}: WIP on main: a1b2c3d incremental orders work
# stash@{1}: WIP on feature: e4f5g6h temp schema changes
# stash@{2}: On main: some other experiment

# Apply a specific stash (keeps it in stack)
git stash apply stash@{1}

# Pop a specific stash (apply + remove)
git stash pop stash@{1}

# See what's IN a stash without applying
git stash show stash@{1}
git stash show -p stash@{1}    # with full diff

# Drop a stash (delete without applying)
git stash drop stash@{0}

# Clear ALL stashes
git stash clear

Stash + new branch

Realize stashed changes deserve their own branch?

git stash branch feature/recovered-work
# Creates a new branch from where you stashed
# Applies the stash to it
# Removes the stash from the list
★ STASH BEST PRACTICES
  • Use messages: git stash push -m "what this is" — future you will thank you
  • Don't let stashes accumulate — they're easy to forget; review weekly
  • For longer-term WIP, create a real branch instead
  • Stashes are LOCAL only — they don't push to GitHub
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Urgent hotfix mid-feature
# You're deep in feature/incremental-orders
# Slack ping: production fct_orders is broken NOW

# 1. Stash current work
git stash push -m "WIP: adding incremental config"

# 2. Switch to a hotfix branch off main
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c hotfix/null-handling

# 3. Find the bad commit
git log --oneline -10
git show a1b2c3d  # confirm the culprit

# 4. Cherry-pick the revert? Or write a fix:
# Option A: revert the bad commit
git revert a1b2c3d
# Option B: write a fix manually
# ... edit fct_orders.sql ...
git commit -am "fix: handle null amounts in fct_orders"

# 5. Push and merge hotfix
git push -u origin hotfix/null-handling
# Open PR → emergency merge

# 6. Back to feature work
git switch feature/incremental-orders
git stash pop
# Resume where you left off
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • git cherry-pick <hash> = apply one specific commit to current branch
  • Cherry-pick creates a NEW commit with the same changes (different hash)
  • Useful for hotfixes, backports, salvaging from abandoned branches
  • git stash = save WIP without committing
  • git stash pop = apply latest stash and remove it
  • Multiple stashes form a stack: git stash list, git stash pop stash@{N}
  • git stash branch <name> turns a stash into a real branch
  • Always use stash messages so future you knows what's in them

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Local Git is solo Git. Real teams sync work through remotes — GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket. Push, pull, fetch, clone — these four commands are how code moves between your laptop and the cloud, and between you and your team.

What a remote is

A remote is a named alias for a URL pointing to another Git repository — usually on GitHub or GitLab. Every repo cloned from GitHub automatically gets a remote called origin.

REMOTE = NAMED URL
origin = https://github.com/yourorg/dbt-project.git
upstream = https://github.com/originalauthor/dbt-project.git

You can have multiple remotes per repo. origin is just convention for "the main one."

Managing remotes

# List remotes
git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/myorg/dbt.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/myorg/dbt.git (push)

# Add a remote
git remote add upstream https://github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-core.git

# Change a remote URL (e.g., switch from HTTPS to SSH)
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:myorg/dbt.git

# Remove a remote
git remote remove upstream

# Rename a remote
git remote rename origin myorg

Cloning a repository

# Clone via HTTPS (asks for password / token)
git clone https://github.com/myorg/dbt-project.git

# Clone via SSH (uses your SSH key)
git clone git@github.com:myorg/dbt-project.git

# Clone into specific folder name
git clone https://github.com/myorg/dbt-project.git my-folder

# Shallow clone (faster, only recent history)
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/myorg/dbt-project.git
★ SSH vs HTTPS

For daily work, set up SSH keys with GitHub once. Then clones, pushes, pulls don't prompt for credentials. HTTPS requires personal access tokens (PATs) — fine, but more friction. See github.com/settings/keys.

Fetching vs pulling

These are two of the most confused commands in Git:

# FETCH — downloads remote changes but doesn't merge them
# Safe; lets you inspect before integrating
git fetch origin

# See what changed without merging
git log HEAD..origin/main --oneline

# PULL — fetches AND merges into your current branch
# = git fetch + git merge
git pull origin main

# PULL with rebase instead of merge
git pull --rebase origin main
FETCH = DOWNLOAD
PULL = DOWNLOAD + MERGE
git fetch updates your knowledge of the remote.
git pull updates AND merges into your current branch.

Use fetch when you want to review first.
Use pull when you trust the changes and want to integrate.

Pushing branches

# Push current branch (assumes upstream is set)
git push

# Push and set upstream tracking (first time pushing a new branch)
git push -u origin feature/incremental-orders

# Now future pushes/pulls on this branch just need:
git push
git pull

# Push to a different remote/branch
git push origin feature/incremental-orders:main
# (left side = local; right side = remote)

# Force push (⚠ rewrites remote history)
git push --force-with-lease   # safer
git push --force              # dangerous

# Push tags
git push --tags

Tracking branches

A local branch can track a remote branch — Git remembers the link, so git pull and git push know where to go without arguments:

# Set upstream when first pushing
git push -u origin my-branch

# Or set it after the fact
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main main

# See tracking info for all branches
git branch -vv
# * main                          a1b2c3d [origin/main: ahead 2] commit msg
#   feature/incremental-orders    e4f5g6h [origin/feature/incremental-orders] feat: add

The .gitignore file

Never commit secrets, build artifacts, or local config. .gitignore tells Git what to skip:

# Typical dbt project .gitignore:

# dbt artifacts
target/
dbt_packages/
logs/

# Profiles + secrets
profiles.yml
.env
*.pem

# Python
__pycache__/
*.pyc
venv/

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/
.DS_Store

# Specific files
secret_key.txt
!important_file.txt   # ! = negate (don't ignore)
⚠ ALREADY-COMMITTED FILES IGNORED LATE

Adding a pattern to .gitignore only ignores untracked files. If you already committed profiles.yml, you must:

git rm --cached profiles.yml
git commit -m "stop tracking profiles.yml"

Then add to .gitignore. Note: history still contains the file — rotate any leaked secrets!

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — First push of a new branch
# You created a local branch and made commits
git status
# On branch feature/DATA-456-incremental-orders
# nothing to commit, working tree clean

# Push for the first time
git push -u origin feature/DATA-456-incremental-orders
# Enumerating objects: 12, done.
# ...
# To github.com:myorg/dbt-project.git
#  * [new branch]      feature/DATA-456 -> feature/DATA-456
# branch 'feature/DATA-456' set up to track 'origin/feature/DATA-456'

# Future pushes/pulls on this branch:
git push
git pull
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • A remote is a named URL alias — usually called origin
  • git clone = download a repo + set up origin
  • git fetch = download remote changes WITHOUT merging
  • git pull = fetch + merge in one step
  • git push -u origin <branch> = first push of new branch (sets tracking)
  • Use git branch -vv to see tracking relationships
  • Always set up .gitignore early — never commit secrets or artifacts
  • If you committed a secret, rotate it AND remove from history

Pull requests (PRs on GitHub, MRs on GitLab) are the gate to production. Every code change in a real company flows through one. Knowing how to open, review, request, and merge PRs is daily-driver knowledge for any analytics engineer.

What a PR is

A pull request is a proposal: "merge my branch into this other branch." It triggers code review, runs automated checks (CI), and once approved, merges your changes in.

PR WORKFLOW
1. Branch off main → commit → push
2. Open PR on GitHub/GitLab
3. CI runs (dbt build, tests, linting)
4. Reviewers comment / request changes
5. You push fixes; PR auto-updates
6. Approved → merge → branch deleted

Opening a PR

After pushing your branch, GitHub usually shows a "Compare & pull request" button. Or open it manually:

  1. Go to your repo on GitHub
  2. Click the "Pull requests" tab
  3. Click "New pull request"
  4. Choose base branch (usually main) and compare branch (your feature branch)
  5. Write title + description
  6. Click "Create pull request"

Writing a good PR description

## What this PR does
Adds fct_orders as an incremental model with a unique_key on order_id.

## Why
The full refresh was taking 12 minutes daily and slowing the team. Incremental drops it to ~30 seconds typical.

## How
- Set materialized: incremental in config
- Added is_incremental() filter on order_date
- Added unique_key + on_schema_change: append_new_columns
- Updated schema.yml with column tests

## Testing
- ✓ dbt build --select fct_orders passes
- ✓ Tested incremental run with 2 days of new data
- ✓ Output row counts match full refresh

## Related
Closes DATA-456
★ PR DESCRIPTION TEMPLATE

Most teams have a .github/pull_request_template.md that auto-fills the description. If yours doesn't, propose one — saves everyone time.

Requesting reviewers

In the right sidebar of the PR:

  • Reviewers — specific people who should approve
  • Assignees — who's responsible for getting this merged
  • Labels — tagging (e.g., bug, feature, needs-review)
  • Projects / Milestone — track in roadmaps

Responding to review feedback

# Reviewer left comments asking for changes
# Make the changes locally, commit, push:

git add models/marts/fct_orders.sql
git commit -m "address PR feedback: handle nulls in amount"
git push

# Push automatically updates the PR
# CI re-runs; reviewer gets notified

# Optional: mark comments as resolved in GitHub UI

Merge strategies

GitHub offers three merge styles when you click "Merge pull request":

Merge commit Creates merge commit; preserves all commits + branch history. Default behavior.
Squash and merge Combines all PR commits into one commit on main. Clean linear history. Most common for dbt/data teams.
Rebase and merge Replays PR commits on top of main without merge commit. Linear history; preserves individual commits.
★ TEAM CONVENTION

Pick one strategy and stick with it. Most data teams prefer Squash and merge — keeps main history clean and readable. Each PR = one commit on main.

Draft PRs

Want feedback on early work without requesting full review? Open as a draft:

  • Click "Create draft pull request" instead of "Create pull request"
  • CI runs but no review request
  • Convert to ready when you want eyes on it

Closing a PR without merging

# Scroll to bottom of PR → "Close pull request"
# Optionally leave a comment explaining why

# Branch can be deleted manually after
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Full PR lifecycle
# 1. Develop
git switch -c feature/DATA-789-snapshot-customers
# ... build snapshot, run dbt snapshot, test ...
git add snapshots/snp_customers.sql
git commit -m "feat: add customer snapshot with SCD2"
git push -u origin feature/DATA-789-snapshot-customers

# 2. On GitHub: open PR
#    Title: feat: add customer SCD2 snapshot (DATA-789)
#    Description: what/why/how, testing notes, links Jira ticket
#    Reviewers: 1-2 teammates

# 3. CI runs:
#    - dbt build --select snp_customers ✓
#    - SQLFluff lint ✓
#    - dbt project evaluator ✓

# 4. Review feedback:
#    "Can you also test on_schema_change behavior?"
git add snapshots/snp_customers.sql
git commit -m "address feedback: handle schema changes"
git push

# 5. Re-approved → squash and merge
# 6. Branch auto-deleted by GitHub
# 7. Pull main locally:
git switch main
git pull
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • PR = proposal to merge one branch into another, gated by review + CI
  • Push your branch first, then open PR on GitHub/GitLab UI
  • Good PR description: what / why / how / testing / related ticket
  • Push more commits to the PR branch → PR auto-updates
  • Three merge strategies: merge commit, squash, rebase (pick team convention)
  • Draft PRs for early feedback without formal review
  • Branches typically auto-delete after merge

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Forking is how open-source contribution works. Even if you don't contribute to open source, you'll encounter forks: forking a dbt package to fix a bug, forking your team's repo for an experiment, or proposing a change to a public tool. Understanding upstream syncing keeps your fork useful.

What a fork is

A fork is a server-side copy of a repository under your own GitHub account. It's like clone but lives on GitHub — letting you push and open PRs back to the original.

FORK vs CLONE
Clone: local copy on your machine
Fork: server-side copy on GitHub under your account

Typical workflow: fork on GitHub → clone your fork locally → push changes → PR back to upstream

The fork workflow

# 1. On GitHub: click "Fork" button on the upstream repo
#    Creates github.com/YOU/repo from github.com/original/repo

# 2. Clone YOUR fork locally
git clone git@github.com:YOU/repo.git
cd repo

# 3. Add the original as "upstream" remote
git remote add upstream git@github.com:original/repo.git
git remote -v
# origin    git@github.com:YOU/repo.git           (fetch)
# origin    git@github.com:YOU/repo.git           (push)
# upstream  git@github.com:original/repo.git      (fetch)
# upstream  git@github.com:original/repo.git      (push)

# 4. Develop on a feature branch
git switch -c fix/typo-in-readme
# ...edit, commit...

# 5. Push to YOUR fork
git push -u origin fix/typo-in-readme

# 6. On GitHub: open PR from YOUR fork → upstream's main
#    Maintainers review; if approved, merged into upstream

Keeping your fork synced with upstream

Upstream moves on; your fork falls behind. Sync regularly:

# Fetch the latest from upstream
git fetch upstream

# Switch to your main
git switch main

# Merge (or rebase) upstream/main into your main
git merge upstream/main
# or, for cleaner history:
git rebase upstream/main

# Push the updated main to your fork
git push origin main

GitHub also has a "Sync fork" button in the web UI that does this for the default branch with one click.

Open-source contribution etiquette

  1. Read CONTRIBUTING.md first — every serious project has one. Follow it.
  2. Check existing issues + PRs — don't duplicate work.
  3. Open an issue first for big changes — get buy-in before investing time.
  4. Keep PRs small and focused — one logical change per PR.
  5. Match existing style — formatting, naming, comments.
  6. Add tests for code changes — make reviewers' job easy.
  7. Be patient and responsive — maintainers are usually volunteers.

Working with dbt-packages

Common scenario: a dbt package (like dbt_utils) has a bug. Fork → fix → use your fork temporarily → PR upstream:

# In your dbt project's packages.yml:
packages:
  - git: "https://github.com/YOU/dbt_utils.git"
    revision: "fix/the-bug-branch"

# Run dbt deps to install YOUR fork's branch
# Verify the fix works
# Open PR from your fork to dbt-labs/dbt-utils

# After upstream merges, switch back to official package
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
    version: 1.2.0

Pulling someone else's PR locally

Want to test a contributor's PR before reviewing on GitHub?

# If they pushed to a fork branch:
git fetch origin pull/123/head:pr-123
git switch pr-123

# Or use GitHub CLI:
gh pr checkout 123
★ THE GITHUB CLI IS WORTH INSTALLING

brew install gh (or equivalent). Lets you open PRs, comment, merge, checkout PRs from the terminal. Especially fast for repetitive workflows.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Contributing a fix to dbt_utils
# 1. Found a bug in dbt_utils.surrogate_key macro
# 2. Fork github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-utils on GitHub
# 3. Clone YOUR fork
git clone git@github.com:Natasha/dbt-utils.git
cd dbt-utils
git remote add upstream git@github.com:dbt-labs/dbt-utils.git

# 4. Sync with upstream
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main

# 5. Branch + fix
git switch -c fix/surrogate-key-nulls
# ... edit macros/sql/surrogate_key.sql ...
# ... add test in integration_tests/ ...
git add -A
git commit -m "fix: surrogate_key handles null inputs"

# 6. Push to YOUR fork
git push -u origin fix/surrogate-key-nulls

# 7. On GitHub: PR from Natasha/dbt-utils:fix/surrogate-key-nulls
#    → dbt-labs/dbt-utils:main
# 8. Wait for review, iterate, merged 🎉
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Fork = server-side copy of a repo on GitHub under your account
  • Standard pattern: fork → clone → branch → push → PR
  • Add upstream remote to keep your fork in sync
  • Sync regularly: git fetch upstream + merge into your main
  • Read CONTRIBUTING.md before opening PRs to open-source projects
  • You can point dbt at YOUR fork via packages.yml while waiting for upstream merge
  • GitHub CLI (gh) makes terminal-PR workflows much faster

🎯 EXAM TIP
A licence defines reuse rights — MIT, Apache and GPL are the common ones. The rule worth internalising: no licence means no permission. Code with no LICENSE file is under exclusive copyright even when it is public on GitHub, so "I found it in a public repo" is not a defence.

Once your team grows beyond 2-3 people, protected branches and CODEOWNERS files become essential governance tools. They enforce review rules, ensure the right people see the right changes, and prevent accidental destruction of main.

What branch protection does

Branch protection rules block actions on specific branches unless conditions are met. Configured per-repo on GitHub under Settings → Branches.

COMMON PROTECTION RULES
Require PR before merging — no direct pushes to main
Require approvals — N reviewers must approve
Require status checks — CI must pass
Require conversation resolution — all review comments resolved
Require linear history — no merge commits (forces squash or rebase)
Restrict pushes — only specific people / teams can push
Lock branch — read-only

Setting up branch protection

  1. Go to repo Settings → Branches
  2. Click "Add branch protection rule"
  3. Branch name pattern: main (or main, release/*)
  4. Check desired options:
☑ Require a pull request before merging
   ☑ Require approvals: 1
   ☑ Dismiss stale approvals when new commits pushed
   ☑ Require review from Code Owners

☑ Require status checks to pass before merging
   ☑ Require branches to be up to date before merging
   Required checks:
     ☑ dbt-test
     ☑ sqlfluff-lint
     ☑ dbt-project-evaluator

☑ Require conversation resolution before merging
☑ Require linear history
☑ Do not allow bypassing the above settings

CODEOWNERS file

A CODEOWNERS file (at root, in .github/, or docs/) declares who automatically gets review requests for specific paths:

# .github/CODEOWNERS

# Default reviewer for everything
* @data-team-lead

# Marts changes need analytics lead approval
/models/marts/  @analytics-lead @data-team-lead

# Snowflake-specific config needs platform owner
/profiles/  @platform-team
**/macros/snowflake/  @snowflake-experts

# YAML changes (tests, docs) lower bar
*.yml  @data-team

# Dependency upgrades need a specific person
/packages.yml  @senior-engineer
/dbt_project.yml  @senior-engineer

# Sensitive: PII handling code requires security review
**/dim_users.sql  @security-team @data-team-lead
**/dim_customers.sql  @security-team @data-team-lead

How CODEOWNERS works

  • When a PR modifies paths matching an entry, those owners are auto-requested as reviewers
  • If "Require review from Code Owners" is on, their approval is required to merge
  • Multiple owners per path = any of them can approve
  • Order matters: later patterns override earlier ones

Required CI checks

Common dbt CI checks to require:

dbt build (Slim CI) Build + test only models modified in the PR
SQLFluff SQL style + linting
dbt-project-evaluator Checks project conforms to best practices
YAML schema validation Ensures schema.yml files are well-formed
Docs build Verifies dbt docs generate succeeds

Bypass + emergency overrides

Sometimes prod is on fire and you need to merge fast. Two options:

  • Allow administrators to bypass — admins can force-merge (use with restraint)
  • "Do not allow bypassing" — even admins must follow rules. Most secure but rigid.
⚠ DON'T BYPASS LIGHTLY

Every bypass is a small erosion of trust in the process. Use only for true emergencies, and document why in the PR. If you're bypassing weekly, your rules are too strict.

Tag protection

You can also protect tags (especially version tags) to prevent accidental deletion:

  • Settings → Tags → "New rule"
  • Pattern: v* (semantic versions)
  • Restrict who can create / delete

Once a team grows past 1-2 people, you need a branching strategy — rules for what branches exist, what they're for, and how work flows between them. Three dominant patterns exist. Picking the right one for your team size and release cadence saves enormous friction.

The three main strategies

GitHub Flow main + short-lived feature branches. Simple, fast. Best for web apps + dbt projects.
Trunk-Based Development Everyone commits to main daily (with feature flags). Best for advanced teams with strong CI.
GitFlow Multiple long-running branches (main, develop, release/*, hotfix/*). Best for traditional release schedules with versioned products.

GitHub Flow (most common for dbt)

GITHUB FLOW
main is always deployable.
Every change starts as a branch off main.
Open PR → review + CI → merge → deploy. 
# Daily life:

git switch main
git pull
git switch -c feature/short-descriptive-name
# ... work, commit, push ...
# Open PR
# Merge → CI deploys to prod
# Delete branch

Pros: simple, easy onboarding, low overhead. Cons: assumes you can deploy continuously; less suitable when you need versioned releases.

Trunk-Based Development

The "elite teams" pattern, popularized by DORA research and Google/Facebook engineering. Everyone commits to main daily — but unfinished features live behind feature flags so main is always shippable.

# Day 1
git switch main
git pull
# Add feature behind flag
echo "is_new_orders_model_enabled: false" >> dbt_project.yml
# Commit incomplete work directly to main
git commit -am "scaffold new orders model behind flag"
git push

# Day 5: feature complete
# Flip flag in config
# is_new_orders_model_enabled: true

# Deploy

Pros: no long-lived branches, no merge conflicts, fast iteration. Cons: requires excellent testing + feature flag infrastructure.

GitFlow (older, more structured)

GITFLOW BRANCHES
main — production releases only
develop — integration branch for next release
feature/* — branched off develop, merged back
release/* — prep branch for upcoming release
hotfix/* — emergency fixes branched off main 
# GitFlow lifecycle:

# Feature
git switch develop && git pull
git switch -c feature/new-thing
# work, PR → develop

# Release prep (when develop has enough for v1.5.0)
git switch -c release/v1.5.0 develop
# bug fixes only on this branch
# PR release/v1.5.0 → main
git tag v1.5.0
git merge main into develop (sync back)

# Hotfix (production bug)
git switch -c hotfix/critical-bug main
# fix, PR → main
git tag v1.5.1
git merge into develop

Pros: clear release management, supports parallel versions. Cons: complex, lots of long-lived branches, merge nightmares.

Which to pick for your team

Solo / 2-3 people GitHub Flow — overhead matters more than process
Small data team (5-15) GitHub Flow with PR review + dev/prod environments
Mature data team (15+) GitHub Flow + Slim CI + thorough automated testing
Versioned product GitFlow if you support multiple versions in parallel
Continuous deploy + flags Trunk-based with feature toggles

Most dbt teams should use GitHub Flow with two environments (dev/prod) — and Slim CI to test only changed models. Add a staging environment if you have a complex stack.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tags mark specific points in history — usually releases. They're how you say "this exact commit is v1.5.0 in production." dbt projects use tags to pin package versions, mark stable releases, and trigger deployment pipelines.

What a tag is

A tag is a named reference to a specific commit. Unlike branches, tags don't move. Once you tag a commit as v1.5.0, that name stays on that commit forever.

TAG TYPES
Lightweight tag: just a name → commit pointer
Annotated tag: name + commit + tagger + message + signature (preferred for releases)

Creating tags

# Lightweight tag (just a marker)
git tag v1.5.0

# Annotated tag (recommended for releases)
git tag -a v1.5.0 -m "Release 1.5.0: incremental fct_orders"

# Tag a specific past commit
git tag -a v1.4.0 a1b2c3d -m "Release 1.4.0"

# Signed annotated tag (with GPG signature)
git tag -s v1.5.0 -m "Signed release 1.5.0"

Listing and inspecting tags

# List all tags
git tag

# List tags matching a pattern
git tag -l "v1.*"

# Show details of a tag (commit + message)
git show v1.5.0

# Find commits between two tags
git log v1.4.0..v1.5.0 --oneline

Pushing tags

By default, git push does NOT push tags. You need to push them explicitly:

# Push a specific tag
git push origin v1.5.0

# Push ALL local tags
git push --tags

# Push tags along with commits (single command)
git push --follow-tags

Deleting tags

# Delete local tag
git tag -d v1.5.0

# Delete remote tag (two-step)
git push origin --delete v1.5.0
# Or older syntax:
git push origin :refs/tags/v1.5.0
⚠ DON'T DELETE PUBLIC TAGS

Once a tag is pushed and others have pulled it, deleting it causes confusion. People may have it locally; deployment systems may rely on it. Treat published tags as immutable.

Semantic versioning (SemVer)

The standard convention for version numbers:

v MAJOR . MINOR . PATCH
MAJOR — breaking changes (incompatible)
MINOR — new features, backward-compatible
PATCH — bug fixes, backward-compatible

Examples: v1.0.0 → v1.0.1 (patch) → v1.1.0 (minor) → v2.0.0 (major breaking)

For dbt projects: v1.5.0 for a new model release, v1.5.1 for a fix to that release, v2.0.0 when you break downstream contracts.

Pre-release tags

# Common pre-release patterns:
v1.5.0-alpha.1
v1.5.0-beta.2
v1.5.0-rc.1     # release candidate

# Use for testing before stable release

GitHub Releases

GitHub builds on tags: a Release is a tag + release notes + optional binaries. Create one through the GitHub UI or CLI:

# Via GitHub web UI:
# 1. Releases → "Draft a new release"
# 2. Pick tag (or create new)
# 3. Add release notes (auto-generate or write)
# 4. Optionally attach build artifacts
# 5. Publish

# Via GitHub CLI:
gh release create v1.5.0   --title "Release 1.5.0"   --notes "Adds incremental fct_orders. Migration guide..."

Auto-generated release notes

GitHub can auto-generate notes from PRs merged between tags. Configure with .github/release.yml:

# .github/release.yml
changelog:
  categories:
    - title: Breaking Changes 🛠
      labels: [breaking]
    - title: New Features 🎉
      labels: [feature]
    - title: Bug Fixes 🐛
      labels: [bug]
    - title: Documentation 📝
      labels: [docs]
    - title: Other Changes
      labels: ["*"]

dbt package versions

dbt packages are pinned to tags in packages.yml:

# packages.yml
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
    version: 1.2.0           # exact version

  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_date
    version: [">=0.9.0", "<1.0.0"]   # range

  - git: "https://github.com/myorg/internal-utils.git"
    revision: v0.5.0         # git tag
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Releasing dbt v2.0.0
# Project is ready for breaking-change release

# 1. Make sure main is up to date
git switch main
git pull

# 2. Update version in dbt_project.yml
# version: '2.0.0'
git add dbt_project.yml
git commit -m "chore: bump version to 2.0.0"
git push

# 3. Create annotated tag
git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "Release 2.0.0

Breaking changes:
- Renamed dim_users.id to dim_users.user_id
- Removed deprecated fct_legacy_orders

New features:
- Incremental fct_orders
- Customer SCD2 snapshot

Migration guide: see CHANGELOG.md"

# 4. Push commits + tag
git push --follow-tags

# 5. On GitHub: create Release
#    Releases → Draft new release → tag v2.0.0
#    Auto-generate notes
#    Mark as latest
#    Publish

# 6. Downstream teams update packages.yml:
#    version: 2.0.0
# Run dbt deps, migrate per CHANGELOG
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Tags = immutable named references to specific commits
  • Annotated tags (-a) are preferred for releases (have message + author)
  • Tags must be pushed explicitly: git push --follow-tags
  • Never delete public tags — they're contracts
  • Use semantic versioning: vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
  • GitHub Releases = tag + release notes + artifacts
  • Auto-generate notes via .github/release.yml + PR labels
  • dbt packages pin to tags via packages.yml

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Eventually you'll force-push over someone's work, delete a critical branch, or wonder when a regression slipped in. Git has tools for every disaster — reflog, bisect, branch recovery. Knowing they exist before you need them is the difference between a 5-minute fix and a 5-hour panic.

Disaster 1: I deleted a branch with unmerged work

# Find the lost commit hash via reflog
git reflog

# 1a2b3c4 HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from feature/abc to main
# 5d6e7f8 HEAD@{1}: commit: feature work I lost
# ...

# Recover by creating a new branch at the lost commit
git switch -c feature/recovered 5d6e7f8

# Or if it was just dropped from HEAD (not in reflog yet):
git fsck --lost-found
# Shows "dangling" commits — pick the one you need

Disaster 2: I force-pushed and overwrote teammate's commits

# Don't panic. Ask the teammate to:
# 1. Check their local Git — they may still have the lost commits
git reflog

# 2. Push their version back (with --force-with-lease this time)
git push --force-with-lease origin branch-name

# If they're already gone / no local copy:
# Check GitHub's "Activity" tab on the repo — shows all pushes
# Force-push events appear with old + new SHAs
# Recover using: git fetch origin <old-sha> (sometimes)
★ PREVENT WITH --force-with-lease

Always use --force-with-lease instead of --force. It refuses to push if the remote has changes you haven't fetched — protecting you from accidentally overwriting teammates.

Disaster 3: I made a horrible commit on main and pushed it

# DO NOT reset + force-push main (breaks everyone)
# DO use git revert:
git switch main
git revert a1b2c3d           # creates new "undo" commit
git push

# History stays linear; everyone safely pulls the revert

Disaster 4: A regression appeared, but when?

git bisect binary-searches commits to find the one that introduced a bug:

# Start bisect
git bisect start

# Tell Git the current commit is bad
git bisect bad

# Tell Git a known-good commit (e.g., last release)
git bisect good v1.4.0

# Git checks out the middle commit
# Test it (run dbt, run the failing query, etc.)
# Mark it
git bisect good   # or bad

# Git checks out the next midpoint
# Repeat marking until found

# Output:
# a1b2c3d is the first bad commit
# commit a1b2c3d
# Author: ...
# Date: ...
#     refactor: simplify fct_orders join

# Exit bisect
git bisect reset

Automating bisect with a test script

# Save a test script (exit 0 if good, non-0 if bad):
# test.sh
#!/bin/bash
dbt run --select fct_orders --quiet
dbt test --select fct_orders --quiet

# Make it executable
chmod +x test.sh

# Bisect automatically:
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good v1.4.0
git bisect run ./test.sh

# Git runs the script at each midpoint, marks good/bad
# Stops at the first bad commit
git bisect reset

Disaster 5: I accidentally committed credentials

This is serious — even after a force-push, history still contains the secret on remote forks/caches. Process:

# IMMEDIATELY: rotate the secret
# (assume the bad actor already has it)

# 1. Generate new API key / password
# 2. Update where it's used
# 3. THEN clean Git history

# Remove file from all history (BFG Repo-Cleaner is easier than git filter-branch)
# Download BFG: https://rtyley.github.io/bfg-repo-cleaner/

# Mirror clone (no working dir)
git clone --mirror git@github.com:org/repo.git

# Remove the file from all history
bfg --delete-files credentials.json repo.git

# OR remove specific text from all files
bfg --replace-text passwords.txt repo.git

# Clean up
cd repo.git
git reflog expire --expire=now --all
git gc --prune=now --aggressive

# Force-push the cleaned history
git push --force

# IMPORTANT: tell ALL collaborators to re-clone
# Their local copies still have the secret
⚠ HISTORY REWRITES BREAK CLONES

Any history-rewriting operation forces everyone to re-clone. Coordinate with your team before doing this. And remember: the secret was public. Rotate it BEFORE worrying about cleaning history.

Disaster 6: detached HEAD

You see this scary message: "You are in 'detached HEAD' state." Means HEAD points to a commit, not a branch. Nothing's broken — just create a branch before committing:

# Currently detached at some commit
# If you made commits, save them to a branch:
git switch -c recovered-work

# Or, if you just want to go back:
git switch main
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Bisect a dbt regression
# fct_orders started returning wrong totals last week
# Last good run: tag v1.4.0
# Suspect commits: ~40 since then

# 1. Set up bisect
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD            # current is broken
git bisect good v1.4.0         # v1.4.0 was fine

# 2. Git checks out commit ~halfway
# Run dbt + test:
dbt run --select fct_orders
dbt test --select fct_orders
# Pass? git bisect good. Fail? git bisect bad.

# 3. Repeat ~5-6 times (log2 of 40 ≈ 5.3)

# 4. Output:
# a1b2c3d is the first bad commit
# Author: Bob
# Date:   2026-05-10
#     refactor: optimize fct_orders join

# 5. Open PR to revert that commit
git bisect reset
git switch -c fix/revert-fct-orders-regression
git revert a1b2c3d
# Push, open PR, merge
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Deleted branches: recover via git reflog or git fsck --lost-found
  • Force-push disasters: teammate's local copy + reflog can save the day
  • Bad commit on main: git revert (creates new undo commit, safe)
  • git bisect = binary search for the commit that broke things
  • Automate bisect with git bisect run <script>
  • Leaked credentials: ROTATE FIRST, then clean history with BFG Repo-Cleaner
  • History rewrites force everyone to re-clone — coordinate
  • Detached HEAD is fine — just create a branch before committing
  • Always prefer --force-with-lease over --force

You'll spend more time using Git in a dbt context than anywhere else. dbt projects have specific Git patterns: model branches per feature, careful PR review on marts, and never committing the wrong things. Get these right and you'll fit in immediately on any analytics engineering team.

│   ├── CODEOWNERS         ← reviewer routing

├── models/

│   ├── intermediate/      ← int_ models (transformations)
│   └── marts/             ← fct_/dim_ final marts
├── seeds/                 ← static CSV files

├── tests/                 ← custom singular tests
├── .gitignore             ← ignore target/, logs/, profiles

├── packages.yml           ← dependencies

Slim CI for dbt

Slim CI tests only models changed by a PR — using --defer to reference production for unchanged models:

# In CI workflow (e.g., GitHub Actions):

# 1. Fetch production manifest.json from artifact storage
aws s3 cp s3://my-artifacts/prod/manifest.json ./prod_manifest.json

# 2. Build only modified models, defer to prod for others
dbt build   --select state:modified+   --defer   --state ./prod_manifest.json

# Result: PR CI runs in ~2 minutes instead of 30
# Only the models YOU changed are rebuilt
# Tests run on them + on dependencies

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
